questions.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving the Exponential Function
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }10{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}10{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =10\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =10\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-4a}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}) \\  & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-4a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{-4x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{-4x}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-4x}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/ade58ce56684420fb0f00236af50bbb54f76801fc8870e1cce135cbd51f1b726.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }10{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}-\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-4a}) \\  & =10(\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{5{e}^{4}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-2x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-2x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x-1}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-1}}{2}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-2x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2e}({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{2a}}-{e}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{2x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{2x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{2x}}=0$

$$

First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {b}^{\,px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p\operatorname{ln}⁡(b)}{b}^{\,px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{5}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{5}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{-{5}^{-x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{5}^{-x}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{5}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/5949cbdface45cf103ae5bbd14db5d81917c19f3ef82417216e26d2064ca6bd1.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{5}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{5}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}}{\sqrt{3}}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-\sqrt{3}u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{\sqrt{3}a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{\sqrt{3}x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/1c0fc31d392bbaccf9a292553321bd60ccbdb2a02f3675543797f570c4fa0ef1.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{3x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{\sqrt{3}a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2x\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\text{d}x.

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

$$

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{a}=0$

\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{x\cdot {4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{4}^{u}}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{4}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{x\cdot {4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{4}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{4}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{4}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{4}^{-u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{4}^{a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{4}^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{4}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{4}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/e50ca6e9326f5a6146a7a486adcc2d3d5f5c059eae3e2e1b06fbff8664b1c7df.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{x\cdot {4}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{4}^{a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to {0}^{-}$ and $u\to 0$ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\frac{1}{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x-1}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{-\infty }{e}^{3u-1}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{3u-1}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x-1}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{3u-1}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{3u-1}}{3}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{-1}-{e}^{3a-1}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-1}}{3}-\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{3x-1}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{3x-1}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{3x-1}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/6a5fd63a29d7c8f5fba712c7fa6c20620c9a1438750f3197606e726a85666827.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{3/x-1}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{e}^{-1}}{3}-\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{3a-1} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-1}}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3e}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Improper Integral Involving the Exponential Function
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{-1}^{a}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{e}^{-3x}}{3}\,]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-3x}]}_{-1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^{-3x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-3x} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-3x} =0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/bc4ffc41105491f2bd6b37b2482afc64946d8f67f6db83dfa322c400ae4bc2b6.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{\infty }{e}^{-3x} & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }{e}^{-3a}-{e}^{3}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (0-{e}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int b^{\,px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1{p\ln(b)} b^{\,px+q} + C
$$

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{2}^{2x+1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {2}^{1}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{2}^{2x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({2}^{0}-{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=2^{2x}$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 2^{2x} = 0$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 2^{2x} = \infty$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/009f467677932d0ac17e1632c31f4d3aa5271ffe332730d9670e69862b243bef.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {2}^{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{2a}) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=x^4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 4x^3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac 14 \textrm{d}u =x^3\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty$ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{2}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{2}^{-u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{2}^{-u}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{2^x},$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = \infty$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{2^{x}} = 0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/1969145d74662468ec23d458ac1ad0194d51cbf6b026718b7232466e9357efdf.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{3}\cdot {2}^{-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{2}^{a}}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$
